And he built a movement and a machine that few ever thought possible.

_**He started observing the Sabbath. **_

Not as a box to check. Not as a religious performance.

_But as an act of obedience. _

As a way of saying, **_" God, You are enough. And because You are enough, I need not carry the weight of a world that was never mine to hold." _**

Every week -- no matter what -- Charlie stopped.

He turned off the noise. He stepped away from the battlefield.

No email. No media. No work.

He gave his full attention fully to God, his wife Erika, and his children.

It was hard at first -- for someone who carried so much.

But over time, it changed him.

Peter, Elon Musk sparked a __**HUGE**__ conversation on Joe Rogan about immigration policy, government systems, and the real threats to voting...

He highlighted concerns that **open borders allow non-citizens to flood in and affect our democracy, including potentially influencing votes.**

Musk explained: **_“That’s why they want open borders... That’s why some leaders changed their views on borders. That’s the reason—to bring in more people who could affect our systems.”_**

That's why Congress passed the SAVE Act (Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act) in the House — a game-changing bill to require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship before anyone can register to vote.

_But the Senate is stalling_ — _**and we can't let that happen.**_

With millions at stake, we need massive pressure **NOW** to force a vote and _**get the SAVE Act to the President's desk.**_

Backed and authored by **House Freedom Caucus member Rep. Chip Roy** , the SAVE Act fights back against the very threats Elon Musk exposed on Rogan—requiring ironclad citizenship proof to protect your vote.

#
Peter —
When James launched this campaign, we weren’t sure what to expect.
James made the decision to reject corporate PAC money. He knew it could hurt our fundraising. But you can’t run a grassroots campaign for the people while selling Texans out to corporate interests.
It may seem like a hard decision. But there was no question for James that it was the right thing to do. James put his faith in this grassroots team and the people of Texas.
And from day one, the response was overwhelming. Within minutes of launching, an HEB worker named Ashley from Fort Worth gave $25. Then Marisol, a teacher from El Paso, made a $5 contribution, and moments later, Jeremy, a librarian from McAllen, gave a $10 recurring donation...and we were off.
Meanwhile, every single one of our opponents in this race has been filling their war chests with the same corporate money that they built their careers on.
We’ve proudly received more donations from Texans than any single one of our opponents. That’s what a grassroots campaign of, by, and for the people of the Lone Star State looks like.
But time is running out in this race, and the billionaire and corporate PAC money is coming in to drown out all of our voices.
Maybe it doesn’t seem like $5 makes a difference against their millions. But it does. All of it adds up — but only if everybody who believes in this movement plays a role.

body:
A $300B company leaves. Colorado joins WHO networks. Judicial power shifts.
| | | | [](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
---
**February 22, 2026** **SUNDAY NEWS DIGEST**
| | Dear Rocky Mountain Voice family,
There’s a clock ticking in Colorado.
Governor Jared Polis has less than a year left in office. And if this week is any indication, he’s not easing off the gas — he’s accelerating.
In a single news cycle, we watched Colorado’s largest publicly traded company walk out the door and the governor double down on global alliances that many Coloradans deeply distrust.
Let’s start with the economy. [Palantir — valued at $300 billion and Colorado’s largest publicly traded company — officially announced they are moving its headquarters from Denver to Miami.](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) A global tech powerhouse leaves Colorado, and according to the reporting, the governor wasn’t even notified before the announcement.
When billion-dollar companies quietly leave your state, it’s not just a business story. It’s a climate story. A confidence story. A leadership story.
Then there’s the public health decision. After the United States formally withdrew from the World Health Organization, [Governor Polis announced Colorado intends to join the WHO’s Global Outbreak and Response Network.](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) His administration says there’s “no additional cost to taxpayers” — but the question many readers asked this week wasn’t about cost. It was about sovereignty. _Why is Colorado aligning itself more closely with an international body that the federal government just exited over concerns about accountability and political influence?_
And then came the courts. This week, [Polis appointed Larimer County Chief Judge Susan Blanco to the Colorado Supreme Court.](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) She will serve until 2028, when voters decide whether to retain her. Critics point to controversial rulings—including her 2023 administrative order limiting public access to audio recordings of proceedings (favoring certified transcripts only)—and question the long-term judicial direction of a court increasingly shaped by one governor.
These stories resonated because people feel something shifting in Colorado. Businesses leaving. Global partnerships expanding. Courts being reshaped. Cultural fights intensifying.
And yes — our two biggest OG stories this week hit that nerve, too.
The [Zyntex story](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) ignited debate over what’s really driving Colorado’s regulatory priorities and who benefits from them. And our [abortion investigation](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) — which revealed how nearly half of one nonprofit’s program funds were spent bringing women in from out of state — struck a chord across the political spectrum. At the same time, a new law tying Medicaid funding to Colorado’s constitutional “right” to abortion went into effect in January, raising even more questions about taxpayer dollars and transparency.
If you haven’t watched our social video breaking that down, [you can find it here.](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)
As Governor Polis approaches the end of his term, Coloradans deserve clarity on the direction of our state. Are we strengthening local control and economic competitiveness — or drifting toward centralized decision-making and policies that push employers and families elsewhere?
The viral response this week tells us something important: people are paying attention. And so are we.
Stay sharp. Stay informed. And stay in the fight.
In truth & liberty, Team RMV

**[Gov. Polis Seeks Answers As Colorado’s Largest Publicly Traded Company Leaves for Florida](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**[THE COLORADO SUN](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Valued at $300B, Palantir was the largest publicly traded company in Colorado. CEO Alex Karp recently bought a monastery in Old Snowmass. Palantir Technologies, a government contractor known for mass surveillance technology aided by artificial intelligence, has moved its headquarters out of Denver in favor of the Miami area, the company said Tuesday in a post on X.com.
**[New Study Alleges Hundreds of Thousands of Record Changes After Colorado Election Certification](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**[JOEHOFT.COM](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Tampering with federal election results is against the law, and a new study by Unite4Freedom exposes an explosive problem—federal election records of the vote are changing after the election has been certified. Is this Malice, ignorance or pathetically pervasive Apathy (MIA) by our election officials?
**[Polis Joins Other Blue States And Aligns Colorado With WHO Global Health Network](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**[COLORADO PUBLIC RADIO](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Last month, the Trump administration announced a breakup: its official withdrawal of the United States from the World Health Organization. The president initiated the split with an executive order on the first day in office of his second term.

**LEGISLATIVE SESSION**
_**Quick Summary of the Week:**_ _This week in the**House** , Democrats advanced a controversial expansion of Colorado’s “ghost gun” law that Republicans argue threatens First and Second Amendment rights by criminalizing common tools and certain digital file sharing. Several bipartisan bills also moved forward. Lawmakers are preparing to debate election-integrity proposals, transit tax diversion zones, pet-store bans, and background-check changes tied to non-citizens._ __
_In the**Senate** , SB 26-018 passed Judiciary on a party-line vote, but Republicans successfully removed the family law provision — a key narrowing of the bill. Budget supplementals are underway, with Republicans raising concerns that funding priorities favor undocumented immigrants over Colorado seniors._____
__
_**This upcoming week:** Another busy stretch at the Capitol with major hearings on election policy, immunization liability, housing and transit incentives, energy regulations, school policies, and cottage food expansion. Testimony opportunities are open — Coloradans must sign up before hearings begin._ __

**[Colorado Democrats Push To Legalize Prostitution Statewide By July](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**[DENVER GAZETTE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) A group of Democrats is seeking to legalize prostitution in Colorado, arguing that current penalties “endanger” consenting adults. The proposal, if enacted, would decriminalize prostitution statewide and preempt local ordinances that ban it. __
**[Democrats advance gun barrel regulation bill on party line vote](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Gun barrels are not serialized. They are not a regulated “firearm” under federal law. But Colorado lawmakers are preparing to vote on whether they should be treated more like one. The bill sponsored by Sen. Tom Sullivan of Centennial, would require barrels to be sold through a federally licensed dealer instead of privately. __
**[Democrats Push Sweeping Tax Plan Reversing Federal Tax Benefits For Colorado Business](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**[THE SUM & SUBSTANCE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Democratic legislators are poised to unveil a quartet of bills next week that could decouple Colorado law from hundreds of millions of dollars in new federal tax breaks, end tax exemptions on downloadable-software sales and rein in several long-standing corporate deductions.

**[At Durango forum, GOP candidates field rotating questions submitted from across Colorado](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**
**[](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.) Instead of posing the same question to an entire panel and allowing candidates to respond in sequence, organizers of the Feb. 13 Republican candidate forum in Durango tried something different. For the most part, candidates received different questions in turn.
**[Speech or statute? Appeals court weighs bond denial in Tina Peters case](https://link.email.rockymountainvoice.)**

clean_body: - Michele Tafoya here! I never really considered running for office. Ever. I was too focused on raising my family, and being the best football sideline reporter I could be. But even in the last few weeks, Minnesota has become the embodiment of everything wrong with politics today. Tim Walz, his inner circle, and the corrupt political class are too busy: Wasting billions of our tax dollars on fraudulent daycares Failing to condemn the activists storming churches Raising prices on hardworking families Sabotaging anything the President wants to do Forcing men into women's spaces Pitting Americans against each other I can 't sit on the sidelines anymore. That's why I'm throwing my hat in the ring and announcing my candidacy for U.S. Senate! thought long and hard about the dynamics of this race before jumping in. Minnesota has long been considered simply out of reach for Republicans. The last time it voted for a GOP President was Nixon. The pundits and political experts say a Republican could never win here. But this year is going to be different for three key reasons: FIRST - I'm running against Tim Walz's right hand. All the rampant fraud that took place here happened under Peggy Flanagan's nose as much as it did under his. We will remind voters about that fact every single day. SECOND - The President has increased his voter share each time he has run. He nearly flipped this state in the last election, and Kamala Harris' running mate was our sitting Governor! Momentum is on our side. THIRD - I'm a different kind of candidate, and I know how to win. I didn't reach the top of my industry by pulling my punches. I put in the work. I never backed down. And I kept fighting, no matter what the naysayers said. In my years on the sidelines, I 've seen a LOT of underdogs win football games that the "experts" said were impossible. The Minnesota Senate race will be another chapter in that storied history. | | ---|--- Thanks in advance for your support. I'll never forget the good folks who stepped up in the opening days of this campaign. You and I are going to do great things together. I can feel it. Be brave. Do good. - Michele Michele Tafoya Republican for Senate, Minnesota It's official - Michele Tafoya is running for U.S. Senate in Minnesota! With the ink still dripping wet on HB 8002 -- rushed through as an "emergency" solution to a sudden housing crisis -- the Connecticut Senate is now slicing up land thinner than a slice of pizza at a child's birthday party.
Nine units on one acre.
_**Children drafting housing policy could have decreed a better bill than this latest proposal being marketed as "starter home" reform.**_
Reducing lot sizes to 5,000 square feet does not magically create affordability. It creates density. And density without infrastructure, environmental safeguards, or affordability requirements is not reform -- it is fantasy.
**Fairfield Is the Preview and their development is not even "starter homes"**
Look at Fairfield.
Businesses that served the community for 40 and 50 years have been displaced for dense redevelopment projects. Downtown corridors reshaped not through organic growth, but through statutory pressure from Hartford.
And this transformation happened before SB151.
It happened under Connecticut General Statutes 8-30g.
**8-30g: The Existing Override**
Section 8-30g already allows developers to override local zoning in municipalities that have not met the state's affordable housing thresholds.
Its practical effects:
* Increased density beyond local planning norms
* Litigation leverage favoring developers
* Pressure to approve projects despite infrastructure strain
* Transformation of established neighborhoods under the "affordability" fantasy

At least 8-30g ties density relief to affordability requirements.
SB151 does not.
**What SB151 Does**
Senate Bill 151:
* Caps lot sizes at 5,000 square feet (up to 9 units per acre)
* Reduces setbacks to 5-10 feet (you can reach out and touch your neighbor)
* Eliminates meaningful height and lot coverage limits
* Mandates zoning changes in areas with existing or "planned" sewer and water
* Provides no state funding for infrastructure upgrades
* Contains no mandatory affordability requirements
* Limits municipalities from acting on public health and safety concerns unless threats are deemed "immediate"
* Weakens historic preservation protections

Combined with HB 8002's parking reductions, SB151 risks:
* Traffic congestion
* Emergency vehicle access challenges
* Overcrowded schools
* Sewer and water system strain (and backup issues)
* Increased stormwater runoff and flooding

And when infrastructure fails?
Local taxpayers pay and it will fail. Towns already have pumping issues to move sewage.
**Density Without Affordability**
If 8-30g was the wedge, SB151 is the sledgehammer.
Under 8-30g, developers receive override benefits only if affordability thresholds are met.
Under SB151, density becomes automatic in sewered areas -- even if sewer expansion is conceptual, unfunded, or years away -- without requiring affordability in return.
That means:
* Naturally occurring affordable homes may be demolished
* Luxury townhomes may replace modest housing stock
* Property taxes may rise to fund infrastructure shortfalls

Reducing lot size does not reduce construction costs, land costs, material costs, or financing costs. You should watch the testimony of Senator Jason Perillo [here](https://substack.com/redirect/277ecd14-26f6-4f54-853b-a98390f4c8ce?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Real affordability requires:
* Sensible Infrastructure investment
* Incentives aligned with middle-class homeownership
* Inclusionary requirements
* Environmental protection
* Local input (Not mandates from Hartford)

**The Bigger Picture**
The Connecticut Legislature -- led by Governor Ned Lamont -- is advancing a vision of housing reform that prioritizes mandates over municipal partnership.
Fairfield is not theoretical.
It is the case study.
Layer 8-30g.
Add HB 8002.
Now impose SB151.
The cumulative effect is not incremental.
It is a recipe for exponential disaster, especially when public transportation is a fantasy.
And if children can see that nine houses crammed onto one acre without affordability requirements doesn't solve a housing crisis, perhaps Hartford should take a breath before reshaping every town in the state.
**Take Action**
The bipartisan grassroots organization CT169 Strong has made it easy to contact legislators and voice opposition.

If you know your representatives' emails, you can copy the message below and send it directly.
**📩 TEXT TO SUBMIT TO YOUR ELECTED OFFICIALS**
Dear Housing Committee, State Reps. and Senators, Legislative Leaders and Gov. Lamont:
Please oppose Senate Bill 151, which eliminates local zoning discretion in areas with existing or planned public sewer and water with top-down state mandates.
Concerns:
1. Caps lot sizes at 5,000 sq ft (9 units or 0.11 per acre), causing exponential density development without evaluating sewer, water, stormwater runoff, schools, roads and parking capacity.
2. Reduces setbacks to 5-10 feet and eliminates height and lot coverage limits, encouraging overcrowding and loss of green space. Developers will maximize profits with oversized luxury developments, not starter or senior homes.
3. Provides no state funding for infrastructure upgrades, shifting costs to local taxpayers and increasing property taxes.
4. Ignores environmental risks including flooding, runoff, tree loss, and water quality damage.
5. Forces townhomes in single-family zones and subdivision of existing lots, limiting municipalities' ability to craft effective affordable housing policies.
6. Contains no affordability requirements and risks demolishing naturally occurring affordable homes to build dense luxury developments.
7. Combined with HB 8002 parking limits, will worsen congestion, safety risks, and emergency access.
8. Mandates zoning based on outdated or unfunded sewer and water expansion plans, potentially increasing local property taxes.
9. Weakens historic preservation protections.
10. Limits municipalities from addressing public health and safety concerns unless threats are deemed "immediate."

Effective housing policy must include local input, infrastructure planning, environmental protection, and real affordability solutions. Senate Bill 151 fails to meet these standards.
Sincerely,
Connecticut Resident

Businesses that served the community for 40 and 50 years have been displaced for dense redevelopment projects. Downtown corridors reshaped not through organic growth, but through statutory pressure from Hartford. And this transformation happened before SB151. It happened under Connecticut General Statutes 8-30g. 8-30g: The Existing Override Section 8-30g already allows developers to override local zoning in municipalities that have not met the state's affordable housing thresholds. Its practical effects: Increased density beyond local planning norms Litigation leverage favoring developers Pressure to approve projects despite infrastructure strain Transformation of established neighborhoods under the "affordability" fantasy At least 8-30g ties density relief to affordability requirements. SB151 does not. What SB151 Does Senate Bill 151: Caps lot sizes at 5,000 square feet (up to 9 units per acre) Reduces setbacks to 5-10 feet (you can reach out and touch your neighbor) Eliminates meaningful height and lot coverage limits Mandates zoning changes in areas with existing or "planned" sewer and water Provides no state funding for infrastructure upgrades Contains no mandatory affordability requirements Limits municipalities from acting on public health and safety concerns unless threats are deemed "immediate" Weakens historic preservation protections Combined with HB 8002's parking reductions, SB151 risks: Traffic congestion Emergency vehicle access challenges Overcrowded schools Sewer and water system strain (and backup issues) Increased stormwater runoff and flooding And when infrastructure fails? Local taxpayers pay and it will fail. Towns already have pumping issues to move sewage. Density Without Affordability If 8-30g was the wedge, SB151 is the sledgehammer. Under 8-30g, developers receive override benefits only if affordability thresholds are met. Under SB151, density becomes automatic in sewered areas -- even if sewer expansion is conceptual, unfunded, or years away -- without requiring affordability in return. That means: Naturally occurring affordable homes may be demolished Luxury townhomes may replace modest housing stock Property taxes may rise to fund infrastructure shortfalls Reducing lot size does not reduce construction costs, land costs, material costs, or financing costs. You should watch the testimony of Senator Jason Perillo . Real affordability requires: Sensible Infrastructure investment Incentives aligned with middle-class homeownership Inclusionary requirements Environmental protection Local input (Not mandates from Hartford) The Bigger Picture The Connecticut Legislature -- led by Governor Ned Lamont -- is advancing a vision of housing reform that prioritizes mandates over municipal partnership. Fairfield is not theoretical. It is the case study. Layer 8-30g. Add HB 8002. Now impose SB151. The cumulative effect is not incremental. It is a recipe for exponential disaster, especially when public transportation is a fantasy. And if children can see that nine houses crammed onto one acre without affordability requirements doesn't solve a housing crisis, perhaps Hartford should take a breath before reshaping every town in the state. Take Action The bipartisan grassroots organization CT169 Strong has made it easy to contact legislators and voice opposition. | | ---|---|--- 👉 Sign the petition and contact your elected officials : If you know your representatives' emails, you can copy the message below and send it directly. 📩 TEXT TO SUBMIT TO YOUR ELECTED OFFICIALS Dear Housing Committee, State Reps. and Senators, Legislative Leaders and Gov. Lamont: Please oppose Senate Bill 151, which eliminates local zoning discretion in areas with existing or planned public sewer and water with top-down state mandates. Concerns: 1. Caps lot sizes at 5,000 sq ft (9 units or 0.11 per acre), causing exponential density development without evaluating sewer, water, stormwater runoff, schools, roads and parking capacity. 2. Reduces setbacks to 5-10 feet and eliminates height and lot coverage limits, encouraging overcrowding and loss of green space. Developers will maximize profits with oversized luxury developments, not starter or senior homes. 3. Provides no state funding for infrastructure upgrades, shifting costs to local taxpayers and increasing property taxes. 4. Ignores environmental risks including flooding, runoff, tree loss, and water quality damage. 5. Forces townhomes in single-family zones and subdivision of existing lots, limiting municipalities' ability to craft effective affordable housing policies. 6. Contains no affordability requirements and risks demolishing naturally occurring affordable homes to build dense luxury developments. 7. Combined with HB 8002 parking limits, will worsen congestion, safety risks, and emergency access. 8. Mandates zoning based on outdated or unfunded sewer and water expansion plans, potentially increasing local property taxes. 9. Weakens historic preservation protections. 10. Limits municipalities from addressing public health and safety concerns unless threats are deemed "immediate." Effective housing policy must include local input, infrastructure planning, environmental protection, and real affordability solutions. Senate Bill 151 fails to meet these standards. Sincerely, Connecticut Resident Nine houses on one acre may look good in a legislative talking point. But it does not make housing affordable -- and it does not make Connecticut stronger. | A guest post by| Consultant, Political Consultant, Campaign Manager, Construction Consultant and Corporate Attorney. Hi,
This is Kimmie, Brandon Herrera's campaign manager.
I've had a front-row seat to this wild ride. This is a massive district - it takes eight hours to drive from one end to the other and includes 27 counties. But Brandon has held a town hall in every county at least once in the final weeks of the campaign, and no other candidate in the country is working harder than our guy to lock down victory.
We're really grateful to you for helping us with your financial support, and we wanted to share another way you can help: send postcards!
It's really easy and a fun way to show off the part of the world you're from. And it's incredibly effective. People often throw conventional political mailers in the trash, but everybody reads a handwritten postcard.
Here are the steps:
1\. Visit our postcard project page at [https://BrandonHerreraforCongress.com/Postcards](https://contact.brandonherreraforcongress.com/l/6fI53a1vdu7637OWRF387YCA/Z3kN8t892JJBSwAe8927iMJThQ/IM27QShsSvO6gUXqXdIu3w) and request your ten addresses.
2\. Get ten postcards and stamps. You can choose postcards that capture what makes home unique and special, but any postcard will do!
3\. Write a **positive** message encouraging the voter to support Brandon. Ask them to make a plan to vote and encourage them to go to BrandonHerreraforCongress.com/Vote for more information.
4\. [Optional] Before you drop the postcards in the mail, we encourage you to take a photo of them and post them on X with the hashtag #BrandonPostcards. Alternatively, you can email the photo to me. We may feature these shared photos in an upcoming video or on the campaign's social media accounts.
Election Day is March 3rd, so please get your postcards out ASAP. They can help elect the next great Congressman from the state of Texas, Brandon Herrera.
Onward,

Kimmie

| For Immediate Release February 23, 2026 Ohio Senate Leaders Endorse Riedel for State Senate President Pro Tempore Bill Reineke, Majority Floor Leader Theresa Gavarone, and Majority Whip George Lang Back the Conservative Choice in the 1st District DEFIANCE - Ohio Senate President Pro Tempore Bill Reineke (R-Tiffin), Senate Majority Floor Leader Theresa Gavarone (R-Bowling Green), and Senate Majority Whip George Lang (R-West Chester) announced their endorsement of Craig Riedel for Ohio's 1st Senate District. Riedel served with Senators Reineke, Gavarone, and Lang in the Ohio House. "Ohio needs decisive leaders with the vision and drive to deliver results," said Senator Reineke. "Craig Riedel has an exceptional private sector background and brings an outsider's approach to Columbus. Northwest Ohio should continue to have a strong conservative representing the 1st Senate District, and that's why I am proud to endorse Craig Riedel." "Northwest Ohio needs strong conservative fighters in the Ohio Senate," said Senator Gavarone. "Craig Riedel has a consistent record of supporting tax cuts, safeguarding women's sports, and opposing Green New Deal policies. I am proud to support conservative outsider Craig Riedel for Ohio's 1st Senate District." "Craig Riedel knows what's needed to make Ohio the most business-friendly state in the country," said Senator Lang. "Craig will work to eliminate Ohio's income tax and slash burdensome regulations on businesses - and he will never waver in defending our conservative values. He has my full support." Riedel issued the following statement upon receiving the endorsements of Senators Reineke, Gavarone, and Lang: "I am deeply humbled to have earned the support of these outstanding leaders in the Ohio Senate. Bill, Theresa, George, and I share a private sector background, which made us an effective team in the Ohio House. I'm proud of what we accomplished together to make our state more business-friendly, and I am excited for the opportunity to continue working alongside them in the Senate." Riedel has previously announced a number of key endorsements from leading conservative organizations, including Ohio Value Voters, Associated Builders and Contractors of Ohio, and Americans for Prosperity-Ohio. He has been certified by the Hancock County Board of Elections as a candidate for the May 5, 2026 Republican primary ballot.
The 1st Senate District encompasses all or parts of 10 counties in Northwest Ohio: all of Defiance, Fulton, Hancock, Hardin, Henry, Paulding, Putnam, Van Wert, and Williams Counties, and part of Logan County. Senate President Rob McColley (R-Napoleon) is term-limited in 2026. Craig and his wife of 37 years, Danette, reside in Defiance. They have two children and three granddaughters. Riedel served as State Representative for the 82nd Ohio House District for six years. A civil engineer, he spent 27 years in the steel industry at Nucor Vulcraft Group.

## Team USA Tops Canada For Hockey Gold
Team USA beat Canada 2-1 in an instant classic gold medal hockey match yesterday morning, a fitting bookend to close out the 2026 Winter Olympics. A heroic defensive effort in the third period forced overtime, setting up an iconic game-winning goal by 24-year-old Jack Hughes to give the Americans gold. [See the](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0D1u6zAQBODTUJ2N5fJPr2DxkkCdnTKlQJEra2PKNCTGjm4fKFdIN_iKGWA-Tv0pcObb5Rxm8nUs_Y2ea6Zaaek50lTilbZLySmX3bbK8Uo9AtoD4AFVnwLnrddN8iMRkmrIS-dkq3XrZDN5N8YwmDRAqyFEk0YzmH-WZBtQaVC2Yb-3AaKSEpyRR1I2RGfdIBPJIbZCAyWuZTl-Fr7Vica8lQctx1jmJvup1vsq1H-BncDue1eB3fnl9T1v853jKrBba6hfe0BAY0FqYxG0cQYAhOpWod4QmsWn-5Nz5tU6oeEyB86_I_VPzzw8_gQAAP__BsJz5g)[ shot](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0D1u6zAQBODTUJ2N5fJPr2DxkkCdnTKlQJEra2PKNCTGjm4fKFdIN_iKGWA-Tv0pcObb5Rxm8nUs_Y2ea6Zaaek50lTilbZLySmX3bbK8Uo9AtoD4AFVnwLnrddN8iMRkmrIS-dkq3XrZDN5N8YwmDRAqyFEk0YzmH-WZBtQaVC2Yb-3AaKSEpyRR1I2RGfdIBPJIbZCAyWuZTl-Fr7Vica8lQctx1jmJvup1vsq1H-BncDue1eB3fnl9T1v853jKrBba6hfe0BAY0FqYxG0cQYAhOpWod4QmsWn-5Nz5tU6oeEyB86_I_VPzzw8_gQAAP__BsJz5g).

The final shot deserves headlines, but the game's most valuable player may have been U.S. goaltender Connor Hellebuyck, who made 41 saves in all, including a [reach-back stop](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuwyAQxvGnwVsi7gAfGRgqVd5SdajU0SJwjmmIiQxN6rev0lfo-hu-T_p_HsejTzkt5zd_ZdemMi78qJlb43VMgecSLrydS465PG1rKVx4RIn9TuIO1Rh9ytuou-gmZmTVsQMisFpbgm52AIEnNgZJ0gmNJfIASMZDBNITdMk91ySiApBkYM-q94F6OkFkOAUrtOSYWln3XyUtbeYpb-XO6z6Ua5fd3NqtCvUicBA4_DxV4PDu11iW4_bhLyxwqM237ypwQInG2ENvjSalDvYgpVBDFeoVZbe6eHuknFPtSWh5vvqU_17av9LcHf4GAAD__-oJc9g) that some observers are hailing as one of the greatest saves ever.

_"This is all about our country. I love the USA, I love my teammates, "_ said a teary-eyed (and now toothless) Jack Hughes after the game, _" I'm so proud to be an American today." _[See the interview here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLHOozAQhJ8GOpC9NhgKF9fQ5dorkWNv8CYGR_ZeIt7-xL3C345GM_q-P7f15ijRsf12O1p-5PXAb03IjGUljzH7F55bTiHlKzuZ_AtXEDB2AjpQa3CUzlW3wT4QAVWLVhojJ60nI9toUYnpPg_z7B1IPwijJc7BTcMwwTDM0JK91gSAklKYQfaoRufNaO4yoLz7qdECA3Eu_TPTwREf6cwfLL3Pe5tsZH7XRv1qYGlgqe9cuPanizlfhQYWV5h8wtrA8nT-1cW_W8Ta0b5jIMfYFXSeKR_dxYlHJ0elQRil-8h7aosN7y-lRHU0jRbb7ij9_-YfCftY-BcAAP__eOl_2Q) _._

It's the first U.S. gold medal in men's hockey since the [Miracle on Ice](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL1ugzAUhZ_GbEb44vhn8NCFLV07Ise-YDeXGIETxNtXaR-h69HROZ--r-t49ZnyY_70C7o6lfGBx05YK25jDphKuOM5F4pU3tlZc7jjCB0o3gGHfow-0znKJroJEbBv0AmthZHSaNEkZ6IUwUYrRDQ3FYySGBVaf7HShsnKJrv3WgfQC9Hpi2ixVz5opW8iorgFw2SHMdeytd8lP2rCic7ywq0NZWnIpVrXnfUfDAYGw3Ec7XP_w06eqEyTX_BdZTCsfkYGw57KwWAwvbgo4DUhF9Z0_Ml3Xuhc1hx4Rb80m4vrkYnyrjST3bz4TL-n9V-mXg5-AgAA__9EcH0e) in 1980, ending a 46-year drought. It's also the first time that the U.S. men's and women's teams have won gold in the same Olympics--_both_ prevailing over the Canadians. Sore-ee!
## Armed Intruder Killed at Mar-a-Lago
A North Carolina man was [shot and killed](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0DFvgzAQBeBfYzYi30F8ZPDQhS1dOyIHH3DNgRG4ifj3Ff0LXd-TPum9r3t3D6KyjJ9hZp-H1C383pVz5q2TnqfUP_kYk0ZNZ3Zk6Z_coUVXWiyx6mIQPbq6iH5gRq4K9kAETV03BMXkI2PTDEgO-EqBKr4BOcd8JQu3Rw2F-FOziBWApStcuHKhJ0cPiAyPvjG15Sg5bZfvJEueeNAjvXi79Gku1E85r7upPgy2BtuwngPOymCr8mKDbd5-5rWcw1aGUsOYyn1KKcsyFpuP61tUZXdkajvOQfSPzf_64uXxNwAA__8or3Nr) by Secret Service agents and a Palm Beach County deputy after he entered the secure perimeter of President Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate carrying a shotgun and a gas can. Twenty-one-year-old Austin Tucker Martin drove into the secured area early Sunday morning as another vehicle was exiting. When confronted by agents, Martin [put down the gas can but raised the shotgun](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLHO4yAQhJ8Gd0SwdkxSUFzjLtdeaWFY7L1gNgKSyG9_8r3C36xWM9KnmfnzmB-OEuX1t9vRtshzxm9N2BqWmTxu7J94rJxC4lM7GvknzqBglAok9HNwlI556IKNiIB9h1Ybo2_DcDO62-x1AONGZa5RLTDGRftlwQh413c0EUNH9qQpgF5rZa76gv3ovBnNogPqxd_EoDBQ43L5y5TbhjEd_MFy8bx3yW6tvarofwmYBEz5eHFtpyVgOsECJgXnf553lWc_AdPuinQyuZVl3bit7yy_hClQXuXuwu6ypBCkqzJzaZv0rnCi7OTKKUrP71JRutKoNgFTV2x4fSklqqMRg1p3R-l_vvajUT8W_gUAAP__XRKMlg), and law enforcement fired. Martin's family reported him missing, and investigators believe he obtained the shotgun while traveling south to Florida. The president and First Lady were at the White House at the time of the incident. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt praised the Secret Service's response and [criticized Democrats](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkD2OpDAUhE8DmZFt3JgOHGxC1ptuiPzzDG_7YbewBcPtR8wVJq2SSvV9_17zyyJhWv7aDUyNeU5wFoJaYZ_Rw5r9G64lU6B8Z1dF_4ZZcjkwLpns52CRrlm1wUQACX0LRmgtRqVGLdrVRK7d-HB6cE_woKKSWvWPp-qVcjZo3qK517iUvRBcP0QH_WC9HrQTAYTzY6M4BKx57_5nTHWFSFc-YO983loya62f0vR_Gjk1cjrPs4v566a4-0ZOGwS0jZwclAKpMkd2g8IIYi3skwkrekvsgJQ3dmAmSB6YjRV2FsAGuthmd2YZ2SUzTB4DpNruJnxOJMIy6EbxZbNIP4_qrzQeRn4HAAD__1ssikw) for the partial government shutdown affecting the Department of Homeland Security.
## Mexican Military Kills Drug Cartel Leader
Mexican military forces killed Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera Cervantes, the head of the [Jalisco New Generation Cartel](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL2OpDAQhJ_GZEb-YfBM4OASsrn0QtTYDfRMg0fGB8vbr9hX2KxUJZWqvn_P_gnEtE5_YUFfxtSveGyMpWDuKeCcwhvPKXHkdHlnofDG3ijTSmWksX0E4rNvquhHRIO2Qq-d0_emuTtdzd42ITgztrZV6qHBwXBTFqJxN908ANuK_NWmjLFaK3fTNdoWgmvdoCPqIdxFozBSSbl-JVrLjCOfacdch7RU7OdSPpuwf4TphOmO46jDsF0vrlyY7pLCdDslxjWgXPCLQpIvYNpCkisecsIVMxRKqwyQC7J8EzNGuRBTgXzKz3_MJckdmCEXEKarso-fg5hpa51o1LQA8c-k8iuOuzffAQAA__-yXYqe), during a raid in western Mexico on Sunday. The U.S. had a [$15 million bounty](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLEOnDAQRL_GdD7Ziw9zhYs0dJc2JfLZa3BuwcjsHeHvI_ILaVarGelpZn49x6fPlNfpp1_QcSrjisdOyIx1zAHnEt54ToUilUs7OYc3jqCgkwoktGP0mc7RNNElRMC2Qaet1b0xvdXN7NSjt6gSQrTp3tlkWmPCI6E3ffsCbZrsLpoCaLVW9q5v2HY-2M6-dET9Cr0wCmPmUm-_S155xkRn-WK9hbI05GbmbRftDwGDgGE9t7LzZQkYLrCAQcH1X-colaK8KgoYFvyTg19lxb1UllyOVW4frFzk1xP5yl5-1ohV7hknlD4xVunrcsp3Jtpl8JWRJKGPWAUMTXVxOzJR3jsrjJoWn-lfSv6vab8O_gYAAP__cG2O3w) on the drug kingpin, whose organization was designated a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. This should not be controversial.
Democratic candidates should be running on healthcare for all. Not dancing around it. Not soft-pedaling it. Not hiding behind consultant language. Running on it.
The fact that this has somehow become a risky position inside Democratic politics is a failure of nerve and conviction, not policy.
The first time I ran for office, I shied away from it. I was told it was unpopular. I was told it would scare voters. I was told it was too big.
That advice was damn wrong.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8ebac606-8089-4e62-b71d-f2c8405cbd4d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
## **It Is Not an Unpopular Position**
[Recent national polling shows roughly 64 to 66 percent ](https://substack.com/redirect/a5105d0b-ef0f-4b6f-bcf1-28e5ac0e5a7d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)of Americans believe the federal government should ensure that everyone has healthcare coverage. About 65 percent of likely voters say they support a Medicare for All style national health insurance program when asked directly.
Even when you break it down by party, support is not fringe. Large majorities of Democrats support it. Strong majorities of independents support it. Even close to half of Republicans express support for some version of national health insurance when described plainly.
Where Americans tend to divide is not on whether everyone should be covered, but on how the system should be structured.
A government run model typically means a single public insurer or national plan that collects taxes or payroll contributions and pays providers directly, like Medicare expanded to everyone or a Taiwan style system.
A private based model usually keeps multiple insurers in place, but under tighter rules, subsidies, and mandates to guarantee coverage, like Germany's nonprofit sickness funds or a heavily regulated ACA framework.
In other words, the disagreement is often about administration and structure, not about the moral principle of universal coverage itself.
But the core principle that everyone should have coverage is not controversial.
So why are Democratic candidates acting like it is?
* * *
## **We Stopped Fighting After the ACA**
After the Affordable Care Act, something shifted.
With the public option was stripped out, it was felt this was as far as we could go. Democrats declared victory and quietly moved on and for some reason, and that was the end of the serious national conversation.
Almost twenty years later, we still do not have a serious national push from congressional or statewide candidates. Lots of talk about lowering cost but not real solutions. Just milquetoast campaign jargon to get votes.
But, the healthcare is still expensive. Premiums are going up and are still crushing families. And medical security is still tied to people's job.
We wanted healthcare for all and what we have is a fight shifting premium costs a little this way and that way. Meanwhile the system is getting more corrupted.
And candidates are still talking in vague paragraphs about "lowering costs."
I have been to 40 states. There is not a single place in this country where people are not worried about healthcare.
Parents worry about premiums.
Workers worry about losing insurance if they lose their job.
Families with chronic conditions worry about coverage gaps.
There is nothing scarier than thinking that if you get sick, you might go broke.
In a developed country, that should not be normal.
Healthcare should be a basic human right.
* * *
## **The Cost Argument Is Misframed**
Every time this conversation happens, someone says: "If you had a heart attack, where would you want to be treated? The United States! Duh!"
And they are right.
If you need a liver transplant, a lung transplant, advanced oncology treatment, cutting edge surgical innovation, the United States leads in research and development. We produce some of the most advanced medical breakthroughs in the world.
But that is not what is crushing everyday Americans.
The vast majority of people drowning in medical bills are not getting experimental nanotech procedures.
Workers and employers (if the employers even offers insurance) are paying HUGE monthly premiums for the ability to have access IF they need it.
Stitches. Broken legs. Blood work. Annual checkups. Diabetes medication. Antibiotics that have existed for decades. Routine screenings. Primary care visits. Chronic condition management.
This is 100 year old medicine.
And we are pricing it like it is proprietary aerospace engineering.
* * *
## **Start With Basic Healthcare for Everyone**
Here is the argument I am making.
Separate the frontier from the foundation.
Keep funding research. Keep pushing innovation. Keep leading in breakthrough medicine. But basic healthcare services should be **zero cost.**
Zero cost family physicians.
Zero cost annual exams.
Zero cost routine blood panels.
Zero cost management of chronic disease.
Zero cost essential medications that have existed for decades.
You should **not** need thousands of dollars in premiums just to monitor your vitals.
You should **not** need to put a broken leg on a credit card.
You should **not** avoid seeing a doctor because you are afraid of the bill.
We can design a system where foundational care is guaranteed, while advanced elective or cutting edge procedures are structured differently.
* * *
## **The World Is Not Dying Under Universal Systems**
**Japan (** $4,600-$5,000 per capita) operates a mandatory social insurance model with regulated pricing and universal participation.
**Taiwan (** $2,500 per capita**)** runs a single payer national insurance program with centralized claims processing and digital integration (which is excellent BTW. I lived there for 2 years).
**Germany (** $8,000 per capita) uses regulated nonprofit sickness funds.

**France (** $6,000 per capita**)** has national insurance with broad provider choice.

**Brazil (** $1,700 per capita**)** constitutionally guarantees healthcare as a right through a tax funded public system.
Different models. Same principle.
**Universal coverage.**
These countries generally spend **FAAARRRRR** less per capita on healthcare than the United States. The United States spends well over $15,000 per person annually on healthcare, far more than any other developed nation.
Yet our outcomes are not leading the world.
Life expectancy in the United States hovers in the mid to high 70s. Many peer nations are in the low to mid 80s.
And the most troubling number is not total lifespan.
**It is health span.**
Americans spend on average more than 15 years in poor health before death ( see chart below). The average American experiences only about 63 years in good health.
Think about that. **It blew my mind and saddened me when I heard it.**
If life expectancy is around 76 years, and good health ends around 63, that means more than a decade of diminished mobility, chronic illness, and reduced quality of life.
That is not because we lack experimental medical breakthroughs.
That is because we underinvest in prevention, routine care, and early intervention.
* * *
## **Yes, Personal Responsibility Matters**
We also need to talk about food. About synthetic additives. About misleading labeling. About a culture that normalizes sedentary behavior.
Get out and walk.
Lift weights.
Stretch.
Eat vegetables and fruit.
Cook at home.
Individual responsibility matters.
But you need individual responsibility **and** structural access.
If basic healthcare is priced out of reach, you cannot blame people for not catching problems early.
* * *
## **Stop the Political Theater**
Democrats, stop with the consultant language.
Stop hedging your votes.
Stop trying to triangulate every issue into a safe middle paragraph.
Say what you believe.
If you believe healthcare is a right, say it.
If you believe basic healthcare should be free and accessible, say it.
If you believe families should never have to worry about the cost of prevention and primary care, say it....
**And fight for it!**
If you lose a race fighting for something that improves people's lives, so be it.
But what is the point of winning elections and never moving the ball? And, lets ask... have we moved the ball? **Bold** ideas move the ball because people are yearning for them.
Healthcare for all is broadly popular.
And if Republicans ever decide to message seriously on accessible healthcare, it will be extremely popular and they will control the conversation.
Do not lose another widely supported policy because you were afraid to speak clearly.
Run on it! Say it with me!
### Healthcare for all.
## Stay Angry.

Just milquetoast campaign jargon to get votes. But, the healthcare is still expensive. Premiums are going up and are still crushing families. And medical security is still tied to people's job. We wanted healthcare for all and what we have is a fight shifting premium costs a little this way and that way. Meanwhile the system is getting more corrupted. And candidates are still talking in vague paragraphs about "lowering costs." I have been to 40 states. There is not a single place in this country where people are not worried about healthcare. Parents worry about premiums. Workers worry about losing insurance if they lose their job. Families with chronic conditions worry about coverage gaps. There is nothing scarier than thinking that if you get sick, you might go broke. In a developed country, that should not be normal. Healthcare should be a basic human right. The Cost Argument Is Misframed Every time this conversation happens, someone says: "If you had a heart attack, where would you want to be treated? The United States! Duh!" And they are right. If you need a liver transplant, a lung transplant, advanced oncology treatment, cutting edge surgical innovation, the United States leads in research and development. We produce some of the most advanced medical breakthroughs in the world. But that is not what is crushing everyday Americans. The vast majority of people drowning in medical bills are not getting experimental nanotech procedures. Workers and employers (if the employers even offers insurance) are paying HUGE monthly premiums for the ability to have access IF they need it. Stitches. Broken legs. Blood work. Annual checkups. Diabetes medication. Antibiotics that have existed for decades. Routine screenings. Primary care visits. Chronic condition management. This is 100 year old medicine. And we are pricing it like it is proprietary aerospace engineering. Start With Basic Healthcare for Everyone Here is the argument I am making. Separate the frontier from the foundation. Keep funding research. Keep pushing innovation. Keep leading in breakthrough medicine. But basic healthcare services should be zero cost. Zero cost family physicians. Zero cost annual exams. Zero cost routine blood panels. Zero cost management of chronic disease. Zero cost essential medications that have existed for decades. You should not need thousands of dollars in premiums just to monitor your vitals. You should not need to put a broken leg on a credit card. You should not avoid seeing a doctor because you are afraid of the bill. We can design a system where foundational care is guaranteed, while advanced elective or cutting edge procedures are structured differently. The World Is Not Dying Under Universal Systems Japan ( $4,600-$5,000 per capita) operates a mandatory social insurance model with regulated pricing and universal participation. Taiwan ( $2,500 per capita) runs a single payer national insurance program with centralized claims processing and digital integration (which is excellent BTW. I lived there for 2 years). Germany ( $8,000 per capita) uses regulated nonprofit sickness funds. France ( $6,000 per capita) has national insurance with broad provider choice. Brazil ( $1,700 per capita) constitutionally guarantees healthcare as a right through a tax funded public system. Different models. Same principle. Universal coverage. These countries generally spend FAAARRRRR less per capita on healthcare than the United States. The United States spends well over $15,000 per person annually on healthcare, far more than any other developed nation. Yet our outcomes are not leading the world. Life expectancy in the United States hovers in the mid to high 70s. Many peer nations are in the low to mid 80s. And the most troubling number is not total lifespan. It is health span. Americans spend on average more than 15 years in poor health before death ( see chart below). The average American experiences only about 63 years in good health. Think about that. It blew my mind and saddened me when I heard it. If life expectancy is around 76 years, and good health ends around 63, that means more than a decade of diminished mobility, chronic illness, and reduced quality of life. That is not because we lack experimental medical breakthroughs. That is because we underinvest in prevention, routine care, and early intervention. Yes, Personal Responsibility Matters We also need to talk about food. About synthetic additives. About misleading labeling. About a culture that normalizes sedentary behavior. Get out and walk. Lift weights. Stretch. Eat vegetables and fruit. Cook at home. Individual responsibility matters. But you need individual responsibility and structural access. If basic healthcare is priced out of reach, you cannot blame people for not catching problems early. Stop the Political Theater Democrats, stop with the consultant language. Stop hedging your votes. Stop trying to triangulate every issue into a safe middle paragraph. Say what you believe. If you believe healthcare is a right, say it. If you believe basic healthcare should be free and accessible, say it. If you believe families should never have to worry about the cost of prevention and primary care, say it.... And fight for it! If you lose a race fighting for something that improves people's lives, so be it. But what is the point of winning elections and never moving the ball? And, lets ask... have we moved the ball? Bold ideas move the ball because people are yearning for them. Healthcare for all is broadly popular. And if Republicans ever decide to message seriously on accessible healthcare, it will be extremely popular and they will control the conversation. Do not lose another widely supported policy because you were afraid to speak clearly. Run on it! Say it with me! Healthcare for all. Stay Angry. | | ---|---|--- Join otherANGRY DEMOCRATS by support Matt's work. Subscribe and Share! | | | | | | | (C) 2026 Matt Diemer Berea, Ohio ? ?

On Sunday morning, the U.S. men's hockey team beat Canada 2-1 in overtime to win America's first Olympic gold in men's hockey since the 1980 "Miracle on Ice." Jack Hughes ended it with a rocket shot less than three minutes into overtime for a dramatic victory, 46 years in the making.
For me, it was personal. Growing up, hockey was a huge part of my life.

Every weekend, my older brother JJ and I would wake up at 5a.m. and have our dad, Jack "Pop" Murphy, drive us from Northeast Philly to Bucks County for practice, arriving at our local rink & on the ice by 6a.m. So it was special that the three of us watched Team USA at 8a.m. yesterday at my house to witness the unthinkable - bringing home the Gold Medal in Men's Hockey after 46 years. We watched that 1980 game hundreds of times.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..QzrmzqameCej8ip7O7bjqfjS4kT9F12_rWmKjSA88HA?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget-preamble&utm_content=188861191)
The men's overtime win was not the only thing that had us pumped. The women's hockey team also won the gold in OT. It was also very moving how the men's team rallied around their former teammate and South Jersey native Johnny Gaudreau, holding up his #13 jersey and bringing his two daughters onto the ice. Johnny and his brother Matthew were tragically killed a couple years ago riding their bikes in broad daylight the day before their sister's wedding. These two hockey stars from Gloucester Catholic, Boston College, and the NHL were the best among us, so it's hard to even describe the feeling of pride that their former Team USA teammates included them. I am just so damn proud of this team and to be an American. No doubt the brothers were watching down with pride from heaven.

My son Jack, 2018.
Days earlier, America also made me proud with our high court's judgment.
### **Dissecting the Supreme Court Ruling on Trump 's Tariffs**
For the better part of a year, the Trump administration has argued that a 1977 law called the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) gave the President essentially unlimited emergency power to tax every country on earth, at any rate, for any duration, for any reason. On Friday, the Supreme Court struck that down in a 6-3 ruling.
Two of Trump's own appointees--Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett--joined the majority decision. That tells you something about what kind of case this actually was.
On the 250th anniversary of America, it was a good reminder of American democracy in action and of how our framers designed three separate, co-equal branches of government for exactly this reason, so that no single person, regardless of party, could accumulate unchecked power. The Supreme Court did its job, and the system held.
Republicans Mitch McConnell and Chuck Grassley, who was literally in the Senate when the law in question was passed in 1977, praised the ruling and called for Congress to reassert its constitutional role over trade as enumerated in Article I of our Constitution.
When the IEEPA was passed in 1977, it was intended to give presidents economic tools during foreign crises. It lets the president freeze assets, block transactions, and sanction hostile regimes during national emergencies. Presidents have invoked it more than 70 times to sanction Iran, respond to the September 11 attacks, target North Korea, and others.
What no president has ever done in IEEPA's entire 49-year existence before this administration was use it to impose tariffs.
The administration's theory rested on two words buried in the statute: "regulate importation." Those words, the White House argued, gave the president unlimited authority to tax any country, any product, at any rate, for any duration without congressional approval.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/950cf2fd-7efa-4afa-b3ae-ebad345e21b7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

[](https://substack.com/redirect/a32bacf4-5f11-4ee5-a075-0144e57cd0da?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
##
**What Did the Courts Say?**
Chief Justice Roberts wrote in his majority opinion:
> _Based on two words separated by 16 others in IEEPA -- 'regulate' and 'importation' -- the President asserts the independent power to impose tariffs on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time. Those words cannot bear such weight._
You can read the whole [decision](https://substack.com/redirect/cfd9906f-e4c2-445a-a9b6-35b5d121736e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) here.
Chief Justice Roberts also invoked what's called the "major questions doctrine" -- the principle that if Congress wants to hand the executive branch power over decisions of enormous economic consequence, it has to say so explicitly. It can't bury that kind of authority in vague language. The court has applied this same doctrine to strike down Biden's student loan forgiveness program and his vaccine mandate for 84 million workers.
It's worth noting this isn't a one-party problem. In 2023, the Supreme Court struck down President Biden's student loan forgiveness program ruling that the administration could not use a 2003 statute to cancel more than $400 billion in debt under the "major questions" doctrine.
Executive overreach has a way of crossing party lines -- and so does the Court's response to it.
The Biden Administration still proceeded down the student loan forgiveness path unilaterally without Congress and forgave over $188 billion under different statutes. I was never in favor of it then (or now).
Justices Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson reached the same IEEPA conclusion by a different route; they said you don't even need the major questions doctrine here because IEEPA just plainly doesn't authorize tariffs under normal statutory interpretation. Gorsuch wrote a substantial concurrence defending the doctrine itself. Barrett wrote a shorter one, distinguishing her reasoning from Gorsuch's.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7dd69f6e-861f-409a-9f18-e6a1939c2f4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|

## **What Happens to the Money?**
This is where things get complicated.
Let's start with a wild number: $500 million.
That's how much the federal government was collecting in tariffs _per day_ under the emergency powers authority President Trump invoked. The [Penn Wharton Budget Model](https://substack.com/redirect/36c8f9b5-bebd-4a6e-80da-174e269befe9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) puts the total collected somewhere between $130 and $200 billion, with potential refund exposure up to $175 billion. Over 300,000 American importers paid in -- basically a tax -- some passed the cost to consumers, some absorbed it as lost margin.
Now they can start asking for it back. Under customs law, importers have 180 days after their goods clear customs to file a protest with U.S. Customs and Border Protection and request a refund. That clock has been running for months, which means the claims pipeline is about to become extremely crowded, extremely quickly.
Justice Kavanaugh's dissent called this a likely "mess," and that's massively underselling it. But the mess isn't a consequence of Friday's ruling. It's a consequence of collecting half a billion dollars a day under a legal authority that didn't exist.
Reimbursements are unlikely - while IEEPA refunds could be remarkably easy: With almost all duty payments now made electronically, and with every IEEPA-related import assigned a specific tariff code, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) could return most of the money owed to importers, with interest, at the push of a button. In several past cases, CBP has issued automatic blanket refunds covering many years and billions of dollars, and duty refunds in general are a daily occurrence.
BUT - With $2 trillion in deficit spending already in his first year, Congress will not be in a rush to add another 10% to their deficit spending and it's likely the Trump administration will make the refund process as burdensome as possible, requiring every importer to file mounds of paperwork, if not a lawsuit, to get its money back.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/8661db58-31fc-4833-9291-f36c47b5a227?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Source: Penn Wharton Budget Model based on data from U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) DataWeb and CBP.
## **What Comes Next?**
The ruling doesn't end Trump's trade war.
The president has reactively & immediately invoked other statutory authorities that do allow tariffs, just with guardrails attached. Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act allows tariffs after an investigation finds unfair trade practices; Trump used it against China in his first term and Biden continued it. Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act allows tariffs on national security grounds but requires a Commerce Department investigation that can take up to 270 days. Section 122 allows a baseline tariff of up to 15 percent on all trading partners, but only for 150 days.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/c3f24716-0149-4c29-a8c7-83a44e98539d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
_Sourced from[Bruce Mehlman's newsletter](https://substack.com/redirect/91902759-abe7-429f-80c3-d1dd9f975ca7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_: _Six-Chart Sunday - Supremely Disrupted: Trade After IEEPA_
These are real tools. They're just not IEEPA. Each requires steps, investigations, and procedural findings, which is exactly why the administration preferred the emergency statute -- the easy button. The difference between "we can impose any tariff on anyone tomorrow" and "we can impose tariffs after process and findings" is significant, both legally and diplomatically.
Markets seem to understand this. The S&P 500 ticked up modestly after the ruling but didn't surge, because investors know the tariff story isn't over. The uncertainty about IEEPA's legality has simply been replaced by uncertainty about what comes next.
## **Why This Matters Beyond Trade**
For those of us who spent careers in uniform and then in government, this ruling lands differently than a typical policy dispute. Trade policy is not just economics. It is foreign policy -- our soft power. And when a president can impose a 50% tariff on India or a 145% tariff on China by invoking emergency powers with no congressional check, you've fundamentally altered the relationship between American power and its partners, with Congress missing in action even though they have an enumerated say in Article I of the Constitution.
Our allies had already started routing trade around us before Friday's ruling. The EU signed trade agreements with Mercosur and India that explicitly exclude the United States. China posted its highest-ever global trade surplus -- $1.2 trillion in 2025 -- largely because it successfully redirected exports to other markets while we were raising walls. Whatever negotiating leverage the tariffs created came at the cost of long-term credibility as a reliable partner.
Countries don't sign 20-year agreements with a partner whose policy can change overnight. That's not a liberal argument or a conservative one. It's just how republics are supposed to work.

How this affects the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) will be one of the most consequential questions of the next few months.

Earlier this month, I published a Hilco Global Report on U.S.-Mexico trade relations that looks at exactly that. You can [read it here.](https://substack.com/redirect/2dadb930-d3bd-41cc-85c0-9ac5c15d5997?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The next several months will be interesting to monitor. But just like we did for our Team USA hockey teams, let's cheer for America - and hope Congress will get off the sidelines and start doing their constitutional job!

From Olympic gold to the Supreme Court's landmark ruling. Here's what both mean for America in 2026. | | | Feb 23 | | | | | | | | | | | | On Sunday morning, the U.S. men's hockey team beat Canada 2-1 in overtime to win America's first Olympic gold in men's hockey since the 1980 "Miracle on Ice." Jack Hughes ended it with a rocket shot less than three minutes into overtime for a dramatic victory, 46 years in the making. For me, it was personal. Growing up, hockey was a huge part of my life. Every weekend, my older brother JJ and I would wake up at 5a.m. and have our dad, Jack "Pop" Murphy, drive us from Northeast Philly to Bucks County for practice, arriving at our local rink & on the ice by 6a.m. So it was special that the three of us watched Team USA at 8a.m. yesterday at my house to witness the unthinkable - bringing home the Gold Medal in Men's Hockey after 46 years. We watched that 1980 game hundreds of times. The men's overtime win was not the only thing that had us pumped. The women's hockey team also won the gold in OT. It was also very moving how the men's team rallied around their former teammate and South Jersey native Johnny Gaudreau, holding up his #13 jersey and bringing his two daughters onto the ice. Johnny and his brother Matthew were tragically killed a couple years ago riding their bikes in broad daylight the day before their sister's wedding. These two hockey stars from Gloucester Catholic, Boston College, and the NHL were the best among us, so it's hard to even describe the feeling of pride that their former Team USA teammates included them. I am just so damn proud of this team and to be an American. No doubt the brothers were watching down with pride from heaven. | | ---|---|--- My son Jack, 2018. Days earlier, America also made me proud with our high court's judgment. Dissecting the Supreme Court Ruling on Trump 's Tariffs For the better part of a year, the Trump administration has argued that a 1977 law called the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) gave the President essentially unlimited emergency power to tax every country on earth, at any rate, for any duration, for any reason. On Friday, the Supreme Court struck that down in a 6-3 ruling. Two of Trump's own appointees--Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett--joined the majority decision. That tells you something about what kind of case this actually was. On the 250th anniversary of America, it was a good reminder of American democracy in action and of how our framers designed three separate, co-equal branches of government for exactly this reason, so that no single person, regardless of party, could accumulate unchecked power. The Supreme Court did its job, and the system held. Republicans Mitch McConnell and Chuck Grassley, who was literally in the Senate when the law in question was passed in 1977, praised the ruling and called for Congress to reassert its constitutional role over trade as enumerated in Article I of our Constitution. When the IEEPA was passed in 1977, it was intended to give presidents economic tools during foreign crises. It lets the president freeze assets, block transactions, and sanction hostile regimes during national emergencies. Presidents have invoked it more than 70 times to sanction Iran, respond to the September 11 attacks, target North Korea, and others. What no president has ever done in IEEPA's entire 49-year existence before this administration was use it to impose tariffs. The administration's theory rested on two words buried in the statute: "regulate importation." Those words, the White House argued, gave the president unlimited authority to tax any country, any product, at any rate, for any duration without congressional approval. | | ---|---|--- Source: Penn Wharton Budget Model based on data from U.S. International Trade Commission's DataWeb, U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Trade Statistics, and U.S. Department of the Treasury's Daily Treasury Statement. Note: Figure shows the cumulative share of IEEPA revenue as a fraction of total customs duties since Jan 2025. Treasury Statement. What Did the Courts Say? Chief Justice Roberts wrote in his majority opinion: Based on two words separated by 16 others in IEEPA -- 'regulate' and 'importation' -- the President asserts the independent power to impose tariffs on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time. Those words cannot bear such weight. You can read the whole here. Chief Justice Roberts also invoked what's called the "major questions doctrine" -- the principle that if Congress wants to hand the executive branch power over decisions of enormous economic consequence, it has to say so explicitly. It can't bury that kind of authority in vague language. The court has applied this same doctrine to strike down Biden's student loan forgiveness program and his vaccine mandate for 84 million workers. It's worth noting this isn't a one-party problem. In 2023, the Supreme Court struck down President Biden's student loan forgiveness program ruling that the administration could not use a 2003 statute to cancel more than $400 billion in debt under the "major questions" doctrine. Executive overreach has a way of crossing party lines -- and so does the Court's response to it. The Biden Administration still proceeded down the student loan forgiveness path unilaterally without Congress and forgave over $188 billion under different statutes. I was never in favor of it then (or now). Justices Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson reached the same IEEPA conclusion by a different route; they said you don't even need the major questions doctrine here because IEEPA just plainly doesn't authorize tariffs under normal statutory interpretation. Gorsuch wrote a substantial concurrence defending the doctrine itself. Barrett wrote a shorter one, distinguishing her reasoning from Gorsuch's. | | ---|---|--- Source: Penn Wharton Budget Model calculations based on data from U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) DataWeb, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) revenue reports, and U.S. Department of the Treasury's Daily What Happens to the Money? This is where things get complicated. Let's start with a wild number: $500 million. That's how much the federal government was collecting in tariffs per day under the emergency powers authority President Trump invoked. The puts the total collected somewhere between $130 and $200 billion, with potential refund exposure up to $175 billion. Over 300,000 American importers paid in -- basically a tax -- some passed the cost to consumers, some absorbed it as lost margin. Now they can start asking for it back. Under customs law, importers have 180 days after their goods clear customs to file a protest with U.S. Customs and Border Protection and request a refund. That clock has been running for months, which means the claims pipeline is about to become extremely crowded, extremely quickly. Justice Kavanaugh's dissent called this a likely "mess," and that's massively underselling it. But the mess isn't a consequence of Friday's ruling. It's a consequence of collecting half a billion dollars a day under a legal authority that didn't exist. Reimbursements are unlikely - while IEEPA refunds could be remarkably easy: With almost all duty payments now made electronically, and with every IEEPA-related import assigned a specific tariff code, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) could return most of the money owed to importers, with interest, at the push of a button. In several past cases, CBP has issued automatic blanket refunds covering many years and billions of dollars, and duty refunds in general are a daily occurrence. BUT - With $2 trillion in deficit spending already in his first year, Congress will not be in a rush to add another 10% to their deficit spending and it's likely the Trump administration will make the refund process as burdensome as possible, requiring every importer to file mounds of paperwork, if not a lawsuit, to get its money back. | | ---|---|--- Source: Penn Wharton Budget Model based on data from U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) DataWeb and CBP. What Comes Next? The ruling doesn't end Trump's trade war. The president has reactively & immediately invoked other statutory authorities that do allow tariffs, just with guardrails attached. Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act allows tariffs after an investigation finds unfair trade practices; Trump used it against China in his first term and Biden continued it. Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act allows tariffs on national security grounds but requires a Commerce Department investigation that can take up to 270 days. Section 122 allows a baseline tariff of up to 15 percent on all trading partners, but only for 150 days. | | ---|---|--- Sourced from: Six-Chart Sunday - Supremely Disrupted: Trade After IEEPA These are real tools. They're just not IEEPA. Each requires steps, investigations, and procedural findings, which is exactly why the administration preferred the emergency statute -- the easy button. The difference between "we can impose any tariff on anyone tomorrow" and "we can impose tariffs after process and findings" is significant, both legally and diplomatically. Markets seem to understand this. The S&P 500 ticked up modestly after the ruling but didn't surge, because investors know the tariff story isn't over. The uncertainty about IEEPA's legality has simply been replaced by uncertainty about what comes next. Why This Matters Beyond Trade** For those of us who spent careers in uniform and then in government, this ruling lands differently than a typical policy dispute. Trade policy is not just economics. It is foreign policy -- our soft power. And when a president can impose a 50% tariff on India or a 145% tariff on China by invoking emergency powers with no congressional check, you've fundamentally altered the relationship between American power and its partners, with Congress missing in action even though they have an enumerated say in Article I of the Constitution. Our allies had already started routing trade around us before Friday's ruling. The EU signed trade agreements with Mercosur and India that explicitly exclude the United States. China posted its highest-ever global trade surplus -- $1.2 trillion in 2025 -- largely because it successfully redirected exports to other markets while we were raising walls. Whatever negotiating leverage the tariffs created came at the cost of long-term credibility as a reliable partner. Countries don't sign 20-year agreements with a partner whose policy can change overnight. That's not a liberal argument or a conservative one. It's just how republics are supposed to work. How this affects the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) will be one of the most consequential questions of the next few months. Earlier this month, I published a Hilco Global Report on U.S.-Mexico trade relations that looks at exactly that. You can The next several months will be interesting to monitor. But just like we did for our Team USA hockey teams, let's cheer for America - and hope Congress will get off the sidelines and start doing their constitutional job! | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw
